questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Several. First of all I wanted to try going abroad in order to try a different way of studying than what we do in Copenhagen. I wanted to learn a third language, and already had some proficiency in french, and I then chose Paris, and Sorbonne in particular, because of its strong philosophical (especially phenomenological) tradition.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Not too bad, but not easy. I had received a specific date and time where I had to show up at the international relations office in Sorbonne, which was not easy to find, as the place is a maze.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The arrival consisted of finding the international relations office to get my proof of attendance stamped, and I didn't receive too much information regarding the studies or the exchange in general.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: One thing that I think was missing that would have made everything easier was an Erasmus introductary week or day or something, so that you could meet the other students from your field. There was one organization, Parismus, that organized parties and events, but I missed meeting the Erasmus students from philosophy as it would have made everything easier regarding information and organization. Luckily I had inscribed in a two weeks language course where I met two people who took some philosophy courses, with whom I could vent the confusion that arose once in a while.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I got housing through the Fondation Danoise, which is in the Cité Universitaire, a huge area for international students which was actually quite nice, except not in Paris city center, but it only took 20min to get to Sorbonne from there. Furthermore in the Cité they do 'brassage' which is exchange between the houses, so I was actually lliving in the mexican house, which I personally preferred over the danish, as the exchange experience for me also meant that I wanted to experience something else than danish culture for some time. Be sure to apply a lot in advance! I applied in november/december, and went on exchange in january and the only reason I got a place was that somebody had just canceled their stay. I think you have to apply around half a year before maybe.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Sorbonne doesn't have a lot of housing on campus. They do have some dorms that I also applied for, but that's in Clignancourt (or maybe they have several, I'm not sure), which is another campus where 1. and 2. year students have their courses, whereas 3. year students and master students have courses in the old buildings of Sorbonne in the center. I didn't hear a lot of good things about the housing in Clignancourt, but I think it's pretty cheap, and very close to the university if you're planning on taking 1. or 2. year courses. The neighbourhood is a little sketchy though.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Didn't stay there. But as a general advice I can say that housing in Paris is pretty difficult, and quite expensive if you're staying in a studio or normal flat with roommates. Some tips : A shared flat is called a 'colocation' and I think that there are facebook groups for renting rooms that you should check out. Expect to pay 700-1000 for a small room if it's in the center. Furthermore you can rent studios.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I had beforehand decided on a number of courses when I made my learning
agreement.In
the first week of courses it's possible to go to different lectures as it's possible to change your inscription after a week. In order to properly inscribe in the courses at the philosophy institute I went to the office of the secretary and confirmed the courses I wanted to take.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The secretariat was helpful when you went there physically, but France is generally very bureaucratic, and not very digitalized, so a lot of times you have to go somewhere physically to talk with somebody and then they might tell you that you have to talk with somebody else, but it always works out in the end.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try some different courses before making the final choice. Once you inscribe for good after the first week or two, you cannot change your inscriptions and exams. Go talk with the secretary if in doubt.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses where difficult for several reasons. I was not fluent in french when I got there, and it took some time to get used to having courses in french, in the beginning I definetely didn't understand everything, which made it a lot harder. But it seemed to me that the level was also higher than in Copenhagen, maybe because the style of philosophy was a bit different, but also because the things discussed were sometimes hard to grasp.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I think it is safe to say that everything about Sorbonne is just more traditional, including the lectures. There is not so much focus on the pedagogical side of lecturing, and the lectures were more 1-way communication than in Copenhagen, also because there was often 100+ people at lectures. They do however also have TD (Travail dirigé) which is more like the seminars we have at UCPH, where the idea is that everyone should work with the topic in smaller groups. This didn't work so well, as it often became a lecture with fewer people present. That said I think there was something very positive about this more traditional lecture style. The professors seemed to be very engaged in what they were talking about, as it was always something they themselves found very interesting and were working on at the time. Another huge difference from Copenhagen was the fact that they don't have a proper syllabus, only recommended readings which are always books, and more classical books usually. What was recommended to read for a specific course usually span the whole history of philosophy (unless it was a specific history course), and the teachers also included a lot of different authors for the same topic. For example I had a course in metaphysics called 'être et amour' which was mostly about love, where the CM (lecture) professor was mainly going through Plato and Plotin, but also Hegel and Stein, whereas the TD with another professor only went through more recent phenomenological litterature, Husserl, Levinas, and Jean-Luc Marion. The main advantage of this style of teaching was that you could read what you found interesting, and always had the privilege to be reading proper books, and no research papers, which was nice for a change.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Histoire de la philosophie moderne - La certitude comme essence de la vérité
Métaphysique - être et amour
Philosophie de l'art - Arts et pouvoirs 
Option - La nature
Histoire de la philosophie moderne - Critique de la raison pure 
Expression écrite - C1 
Philosophie générale - L'idée du monde

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would definetely recommend the metaphysics course, it was super interesting and really broad in it's scope (being and love) while also being really detailed as the teacher in the CM used 5 weeks to describe love as descibed in Plato. And you also get to read some phenomenology if you take the TD with M. Fournier (there are several seminars with different teachers and different readings).
I also found philosophy of art very interesting, especially because we don't have anything like it in Copenhagen, but at Sorbonne they even have a masters just for philosophy of art. The modern philsophy course I had was very focused on Descartes, which was interesting but also maybe a bit too much Descartes, so unless you really love Descartes, I might recommend to steer out of it, but I personally liked it at times. The professor (M. Carraud) is a super old guy which made his lectures a bit slow, and quite boring, as he would often just quote things in latin or german for 5 min and then use 10 min on translating them and talking about some very niche things. But he's also head of the Descartes research center at Sorbonne, so if you want to learn about Descartes, he's definetely interesting.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had some problems with the phone companies there. I thought I could just use my danish number as it's free in the EU, but it turned out that it was only free for 4 months, so I had to get a french number for the last two. So a good idea is to check whether the same applies for you, or just get a subscription that you can cancel anytime, my mistake was to buy prepaid SIM-cards and try to fill them up which didn't work.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Supermarket prices are around the same, but it's cheaper to go to farmer's markets in weekends than going to the supermarket. The bakeries are super cheap (baguette/tradition = 1,2 eur). It's more expensive to drink beer (but not wine) and to eat kebab (but the libanese ones are delicious). Most museums are free if you're a student and/or under 26!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was a sports programme, but I wasn't enrolled. I don't believe that there was a lot of other things happening, they usually don't do so much at the university, but go out to other places and do stuff.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Museums, cafés. Also I did a language course in the beginning of the semester (offered by Sorbonne) which was where I got some friends, except from the ones from my house.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Museums, reading, go to Bois de Vincennes (I never made it, but heard it was nice). Paris is such a big city, just go to different arrondissements.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy. I was a bit confused as to what to eat in the beginning, as they don't have all the same things in the supermarkets, but that was a minor adjustment.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Good luck, I found it hard, but if you're really good at talking with people, or find someone who wants to speak english then go for it. My conversations with other students where limited to asking about administrative things like how the exams work, or how to write assignments.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Food especially farmer's markets. The art museums of Paris. The cafés and second hand book stores.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Practice french beforehand - the better you are at french the easier it will be to understand the professors, administration, official emails and so on. 
Don't stress too much about the administrative things, but be vigilant as they also do make mistakes (had a friend who weren't on the mailing list of the adminstration, so I had to forward all the mail to her. She even asked to be put on but never got...) 
Get housing in advance.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think I mentioned quite a lot about the differences in administrating the courses, but I think it's important to remember that the learning agreement isn't set in stone, it can be changed when you get there and find out that you would have liked some other courses. Bachelor is called 'licence' in french, and if you're going on exchange on the licence, it is possible to get master courses (even though it may say on a website that it's not), but it might depend on the coordinator in Cophenhagen whether you're allowed to take them or not. The master courses might be a little more chill from what I heard. In general the courses are quite tough and I was honestly scared that I wouldn't pass all of them. The grading system is very different, it goes from 0-20 and you need at least a 10 to pass. The level of work needed to get a 10 is definetely higher that what I would say you would need to get 02 in DK. So expect to get "low" grades. That said, they are more lax with Erasmus students, and don't judge you too hard for making grammar mistakes in the assignments, or for using too simple language. The assignments you make during the year also count towards the final grade, in general I think 50% of the final grade is the exam and 50% is the work you make during the year, so it's definetely better not to slack on those assignments.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Noticing how I got better at understanding the teachers and the books I were reading each week. And in the end being able to write 4-hour exams in hand that weren't that bad. It was also very rewarding to get a new perspective on philosophy and teaching by studying in Paris. It also gave me a renewed confidence in philosophy, as philosophy in Paris is a quite prestigious study, and the professors at the university believe in it 100%, whereas there is a tendency in DK that we need learn how to justify the fact that we study philosophy. Overall it was a boost to my philosophy studies.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to a very different lifestyle without my usual friends and connections. Being content with living a bit more solitary. Writing assignments in french always took me 6-8 hours for a 2-3 pages assignment, as I struggled a lot with using the right expressions. It's a good idea to find someone better at french that can give you some feedback on writing !

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
Good luck and have fun ! 
(In french they always make a space between a sentence and the exclamation or question mark ! Super weird right ?) 
You're welcome to contact me if you decide to go and have questions !

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
